Polar decomposition (A=U∣A∣)

Words: 57
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
For a bounded operator A on a Hilbert space, set ∣A∣=(A∗A)1/2. There is a unique partial isometry U, zero on kerA, satisfying A=U∣A∣; on the range of ∣A∣, define U(∣A∣x)=Ax and extend by continuity. This is well-defined and isometric because ∥Ax∥2=⟨A∗Ax,x⟩=∥∣A∣x∥2. For an invertible square matrix, U is unitary.

Shift operator

Words: 142 Articles: 4
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
A shift operator translates the components of a function or sequence by a fixed displacement. Bilateral shifts act on doubly infinite sequences; the unilateral shift operator acts on a one-sided sequence space and has distinct forward and backward versions.

Unilateral shift operator

Words: 106 Articles: 3
Shift operator OurBigBook.com
The unilateral shifts on sequences move every component one place left or right. Their spectra illustrate behavior absent in finite dimensions.

Left shift operator (L(f1​,f2​,…)=(f2​,f3​,…))

Words: 37
Unilateral shift operator OurBigBook.com
On the Hilbert space ℓ2(N), the left shift deletes the first coordinate. It is the adjoint operator of the unilateral shift operator S. The identities LS=I and SLf=f−f1​e1​ show that it is also the Moore–Penrose inverse of an operator for S; both maps have operator norm one.

Point spectrum (σp​(T))

Words: 11
Unilateral shift operator OurBigBook.com
The point spectrum of an operator is its set of eigenvalues.

Wandering-vector characterization of a unilateral shift

Words: 37
Unilateral shift operator OurBigBook.com
An operator T is a unilateral shift exactly when it is an isometry, (ImT)⊥ is one-dimensional, and ⋂n≥1​Im(Tn)={0}. A unit vector e1​ in the first orthogonal complement is wandering, and en​=Tn−1e1​ is a complete orthonormal basis.

Solvability condition

Words: 79
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
A solvability condition is a compatibility requirement on data for an equation to admit a solution in a specified function space or with specified boundary behavior. For a bounded linear operator between Hilbert spaces, the equation Lu=f requires f to be orthogonal to the kernel of the adjoint. A closed range makes that requirement sufficient; the Fredholm alternative for a compact operator applies this principle to I−K with compact K. in an asymptotic inner problem, exclusion of a growing homogeneous mode can impose an analogous weighted-integral condition.

Spectrum (functional analysis)

Words: 200 Articles: 5
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
The spectrum of a linear operator consists of the scalars λ for which A−λI is not invertible. In finite dimensions it is the set of eigenvalues.

Approximate eigenvalue (λ∈σap​(T))

Words: 56 Articles: 1
Spectrum (functional analysis) OurBigBook.com
An approximate eigenvalue of a bounded operator T is a scalar λ admitting unit vectors xn​ with ∥(T−λI)xn​∥→0. Every approximate eigenvalue belongs to the spectrum; for a normal operator, all spectral points are approximate eigenvalues.

Approximate eigenvector (∥un​∥=1,∥(A−λ)un​∥→0)

Words: 20
Approximate eigenvalue OurBigBook.com
The unit vectors realizing an approximate eigenvalue are approximate eigenvectors: their residual tends to zero, although they need not converge to any genuine eigenvector.

Residual spectrum (σr​(T))

Words: 45
Spectrum (functional analysis) OurBigBook.com
In the disjoint convention for a bounded linear operator T, the residual spectrum consists of λ for which T−λI is injective but has nondense range. Together with the point spectrum and continuous spectrum it partitions the spectrum of a bounded operator. Some conventions also include noninjective operators with nondense range, so the convention must be stated.

Continuous spectrum

Words: 43
Spectrum (functional analysis) OurBigBook.com
For a self-adjoint operator T, a real number λ lies in the continuous spectrum when T−λI is injective with dense range but is not surjective. Such spectral values need not be eigenvalues of normalizable states. The free-particle Hamiltonian on the real line has a continuous energy spectrum.

Spectrum of a bounded operator

Words: 32
Spectrum (functional analysis) OurBigBook.com
For a bounded operator on a complex Banach space, the spectrum is a nonempty compact subset of the complex plane contained in the closed disk of radius equal to the operator norm.

Compression of a linear operator

Words: 46
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
If V is a subspace of a space with an inner product and PV​ is its orthogonal projection, the compression of an operator A to V is
PV​A∣V​:V⟶V.
(1)
If the columns of Z are an orthonormal basis of V, its matrix in that basis is Z∗AZ.

Self-adjoint operator

Words: 894 Articles: 17
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
A densely defined operator T on a Hilbert space is self-adjoint when it equals its adjoint operator, including equality of their operator domains:
D(T)=D(T∗),Tv=T∗v(v∈D(T)).
(2)
For a bounded linear operator defined on the whole Hilbert space, this is equivalent to
⟨Tv,w⟩=⟨v,Tw⟩
(3)
for all vectors v,w. For an unbounded self-adjoint operator, the domain condition is essential: the inner-product identity on D(T) alone gives only a symmetric operator.

Negative-energy direction gives exponential growth in a self-adjoint wave equation (∥q(t)∥≥∥q0​∥eαt)

Words: 124
Self-adjoint operator OurBigBook.com
Let q¨​=Fq on a Hilbert space, with time-independent self-adjoint operator F, and conserved quadratic energy E=∥q˙​∥2/2−⟨q,Fq⟩/2. If ⟨q0​,Fq0​⟩>0, set q˙​(0)=αq0​ with α2=⟨q0​,Fq0​⟩/∥q0​∥2 and α>0. This gives E=0. For N=∥q∥2, N′=2Re⟨q,q˙​⟩ and N′′=4∥q˙​∥2, so
(lnN)′′=N24[N∥q˙​∥2−(Re⟨q,q˙​⟩)2]​≥0
(4)
by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Since (lnN)′(0)=2α, N(t)≥N(0)e2αt. Positivity of N follows from N′(0)>0 and N′′≥0. Thus a negative direction of the restoring energy W=−⟨q,Fq⟩/2 yields an exponentially growing solution without a normal-mode expansion or a variational spectral theorem. If W is positive definite, conserved E instead controls the energy norm; a bound in the original Hilbert space norm additionally follows from a coercive lower bound on W.

Friedrichs extension (AF​)

Words: 82
Self-adjoint operator OurBigBook.com
A densely defined semibounded symmetric operator on a Hilbert space has a canonical semibounded extension that is a self-adjoint operator obtained by closing its quadratic form. After shifting the lower bound to zero, complete the initial form domain in the norm (∥u∥2+q[u])1/2; the associated closed form determines the Friedrichs extension. For the positive Laplace-Beltrami operator on a polygonal surface, this specifies the finite-energy realization at corners. Different choices of the initial form domain impose Dirichlet boundary conditions, Neumann boundary conditions, or mixed boundary conditions; the extension does not choose the boundary condition independently of that domain.

Spectral Weyl sequence (∥fn​∥=1,(L−λI)fn​→0)

Words: 140 Articles: 1
Self-adjoint operator OurBigBook.com
For a bounded self-adjoint operator L, a spectral Weyl sequence at λ consists of unit vectors fn​ with ∥(L−λI)fn​∥→0. Such a sequence exists exactly at points of the spectrum of a bounded operator. If no sequence exists, the shifted operator is bounded below, with closed range and zero kernel. Self-adjointness then makes its range dense, so it is invertible. This spectral criterion is different from the equidistribution Weyl criterion.

Singular Weyl sequence (∥fn​∥=1,fn​⇀0,(L−λI)fn​→0)

Words: 75
Spectral Weyl sequence OurBigBook.com
A singular Weyl sequence for a bounded self-adjoint operator L at λ is a spectral Weyl sequence that also converges weakly to zero. Such a sequence exists exactly when λ is in the essential spectrum of a bounded self-adjoint operator. An infinite-dimensional shifted kernel gives a weakly null orthonormal sequence. If that kernel is finite-dimensional but the shifted range is not closed, choose approximate null vectors in the kernel complement and extract a weakly convergent subsequence; its limit belongs to both kernel and complement, so is zero.

Unbounded self-adjoint operator (A=A∗,D(A)=D(A∗))

Words: 139 Articles: 2
Self-adjoint operator OurBigBook.com
A densely defined linear operator on a complex Hilbert space is self-adjoint when its adjoint operator has exactly the same domain and agrees there. Symmetry only requires A⊆A∗ and does not guarantee self-adjointness. A self-adjoint operator is a closed operator with real spectrum. Domains matter for differential operators and unbounded multiplication operators.

Spectral positivity criterion for a self-adjoint operator (A≥0⟺σ(A)⊆[0,∞))

Words: 47
Unbounded self-adjoint operator OurBigBook.com
Positivity makes A−z bounded below with dense closed range for every z<0, excluding negative spectral values. Conversely if the spectrum is nonnegative, R=(I+A)−1 has spectrum in [0,1] by the resolvent spectral mapping identity. The numerical-range endpoint approximate-eigenvalue theorem gives 0≤R≤I, and positive-form Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives ∥Rf∥2≤⟨Rf,f⟩. For u=Rf, ⟨Au,u⟩=⟨Rf,f⟩−∥Rf∥2≥0.

Nonreal resolvent estimate for a self-adjoint operator (∥(A−z)−1∥≤∣Imz∣−1)

Words: 48
Unbounded self-adjoint operator OurBigBook.com
Symmetry gives ∥(A−z)u∥≥∣Imz∣∥u∥ when z is nonreal. Closedness makes the range closed; its orthogonal complement is ker(A−z)=0, so it is also dense and hence surjective. This proves the resolvent estimate and reality of the spectrum. Equality of the adjoint domains is needed in the range argument.

Fredholm solvability condition for a self-adjoint operator

Words: 55
Self-adjoint operator OurBigBook.com
For a self-adjoint operator L, solving Lu=f requires f to be orthogonal to every v∈kerL, because ⟨v,Lu⟩=⟨Lv,u⟩=0. When the range is closed, this condition is also sufficient: (ranL)⊥=kerL and closedness gives ranL=(kerL)⊥. In finite dimensions the range is automatically closed. This Fredholm solvability condition determines amplitude equations by projecting perturbative forcing onto critical eigenfunctions.

Positive-definite operator (⟨Av,v⟩>0(v=0))

Words: 129 Articles: 1
Self-adjoint operator OurBigBook.com
A self-adjoint operator A is positive definite when ⟨Av,v⟩>0 for every nonzero vector v in its domain. In finite dimension it is invertible and has positive eigenvalues. In infinite dimension, strict positivity of individual quadratic-form values need not give a bounded inverse; the stronger uniform bound ⟨Av,v⟩≥c∥v∥2 with c>0 supplies coercivity.
For maps β:U→V and γ:V→W between finite-dimensional inner product spaces, with imβ=kerγ, the operator ββ∗+γ∗γ is positive definite. Its quadratic form is ∥β∗v∥2+∥γv∥2, whose zero set is imβ∩(imβ)⊥={0}. This uses the adjoint operator relation kerβ∗=(imβ)⊥.

Strict operator positivity does not imply surjectivity

Words: 41
Positive-definite operator OurBigBook.com
On ℓ2, the bounded self-adjoint operator (Lv)j​=vj​/j is strictly positive. Yet fj​=1/j lies in ℓ2 and Lu=f would require the non-square-summable vector uj​=1. A positive uniform lower bound, rather than strict positivity alone, guarantees a bounded inverse for a bounded self-adjoint operator.

Finite-dimensional spectral theorem

Words: 93 Articles: 2
Self-adjoint operator OurBigBook.com
Every self-adjoint operator on a finite-dimensional real inner-product space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors and only real eigenvalues.

Multiplicity-free complete dyadic spectrum

Words: 64
Finite-dimensional spectral theorem OurBigBook.com
A Hermitian operator on a 2n-dimensional Hilbert space, with 2n distinct eigenvalues all belonging to {c/2n:0≤c<2n}, must occupy this entire grid. This follows from the pigeonhole principle: the set of possible values and the set of distinct eigenvalues have the same cardinality. Its minimum eigenvalue is zero, so the operator is necessarily singular. Distinctness therefore does not imply invertibility; it forces a one-dimensional kernel in this specific complete-grid setting.

Orthonormal eigenbasis

Words: 10
Finite-dimensional spectral theorem OurBigBook.com
An orthonormal eigenbasis of a linear operator is an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors.

Operator theory OurBigBook.com
Every real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable. Distinct eigenspaces are orthogonal because symmetry gives λ⟨u,v⟩=μ⟨u,v⟩.

Power method

Words: 404 Articles: 9
Operator theory OurBigBook.com
Iterate q(k+1)=Aq(k)/∥Aq(k)∥. With a unique dominant eigenvalue separated by a spectral gap and a starting vector that is nonorthogonal to its eigenvector, the directions converge at the spectral-ratio rate.
The power method is power iteration; its convergence depends on the dominant spectral component of the starting vector.

Dominant eigenpair extraction from a two-step Krylov recurrence (yk+2​=syk+1​−pyk​)

Words: 58
Power method OurBigBook.com
When two independent iterates span an invariant two-dimensional subspace, their recurrence gives the characteristic polynomial λ2−sλ+p. For distinct roots λ1​,λ2​, corresponding eigenvectors are yk+1​−λ2​yk​ and yk+1​−λ1​yk​. For a merely approximately dominant subspace, the same computation gives approximate eigenpairs. A single orbit cannot separate a repeated eigenvalue's entire eigenspace when its projection is only one direction.

Quadratic Rayleigh-quotient improvement for the power method

Words: 40
Power method OurBigBook.com
For a real symmetric matrix with ∣λ1​∣>∣λ2​∣ and a starting vector having nonzero component in the leading eigendirection, power-method direction errors are
O(​λ1​λ2​​​k),
(8)
whereas the Rayleigh quotient error is
O(​λ1​λ2​​​2k).
(9)
The improvement occurs because orthogonality cancels terms linear in the direction error.

Active spectrum of the power method

Words: 40
Power method OurBigBook.com
The active spectrum consists of eigenvalues whose eigenspaces have nonzero projection of the starting vector. The power method converges toward the eigenvalue of largest modulus in this active spectrum; an exactly absent dominant component is never created in exact arithmetic.

Inverse iteration

Words: 158 Articles: 2
Power method OurBigBook.com
Inverse iteration repeatedly solves (A−sI)yk+1​=qk​ and normalizes. It is the power method for (A−sI)−1 and converges toward an eigenvector whose eigenvalue is closest to the shift s.

Convergence of fixed-shift inverse iteration

Words: 130 Articles: 1
Inverse iteration OurBigBook.com
If A is real symmetric, s is not an eigenvalue, one eigenvalue λ∗​ is uniquely closest to s, and the initial vector has a nonzero component in its eigenspace, fixed-shift inverse iteration converges to that eigenspace. Its asymptotic direction-error ratio is
∣λnext​−s∣∣λ∗​−s∣​,
(10)
where λnext​ is second closest to s.
Sign behavior of fixed-shift inverse iteration
Words: 77
Convergence of fixed-shift inverse iteration OurBigBook.com
If the closest eigenvalue λ∗​ lies above the shift, the dominant eigenvalue (λ∗​−s)−1 of the inverse is positive and normalized iterates approach one fixed sign of its eigenvector. If λ∗​<s, that inverse eigenvalue is negative, so the direction converges but consecutive normalized vectors alternate signs. At a shift exactly midway between two simple eigenvalues, the two inverse eigenvalues have equal modulus and opposite signs, so generic iterates alternate between two mixtures instead of selecting one eigenvector.

Subspace iteration

Words: 67 Articles: 2
Power method OurBigBook.com
Subspace iteration repeatedly applies a matrix to several independent vectors and orthonormalizes them, converging to a dominant invariant subspace when a spectral gap separates the selected eigenvalue cluster.

Dominant invariant subspace

Words: 16
Subspace iteration OurBigBook.com
A dominant invariant subspace is spanned by eigenvectors whose eigenvalue moduli exceed those outside the subspace.

Power method with a dominant eigenvalue cluster

Words: 23
Subspace iteration OurBigBook.com
When several eigenvalues share the largest modulus, normalized power iterates need not converge individually, but every limit lies in their joint invariant subspace.

Largest-eigenvalue interlacing for a principal submatrix (λ1​≥μ1​≥λ2​)

Words: 77
Eigenvalue interlacing OurBigBook.com
Let a real symmetric matrix M have ordered eigenvalues λ1​≥λ2​≥⋯≥λn​, with n≥2. If A is obtained by deleting one matching row and column, its largest eigenvalue μ1​ satisfies
λ1​≥μ1​≥λ2​.

Spectral decomposition OurBigBook.com
A spectral gap is a positive separation between designated parts of the spectrum of a linear operator. For the power method, the relevant gap separates the modulus of the dominant eigenvalue from the other eigenvalue moduli.
Ground-space perturbation bound (δν−δ2/(g−δ)≤λmin​(H+δV)≤δν)
Words: 78
Spectral gap OurBigBook.com
Suppose H≥0 has ground energy zero and positive spectral gap at least g, and 0≤V≤I. Let ν be the minimum of V restricted to the ground space. Splitting a normalized vector into ground and excited components bounds its energy below by δν+(g−δ)y2−2δy, with y the excited norm. Completing the square yields the displayed bound for 0<δ<g. The error is controlled by the gap and cannot be treated as a uniform O(δ2) when g closes.
Davis-Kahan theorem
Words: 148 Articles: 2
Spectral gap OurBigBook.com
The Davis-Kahan theorem bounds the change of an invariant eigenspace of a symmetric matrix in terms of a matrix perturbation and an appropriate spectral gap. The rank-one eigenprojector perturbation bound below depends only on the unperturbed gap. Yu, Wang and Samworth's formulation gives population-gap bounds in greater generality.
Davis-Kahan curvature lemma (2γ​∥P−Q∥F2​≤tr(H(P−Q)))
Words: 108 Articles: 1
Davis-Kahan theorem OurBigBook.com
If a symmetric matrix H has largest eigenvalue λ1​ separated from λ2​ by γ>0, and P=vv⊤ is its leading rank-one orthogonal projection matrix, then every unit vector u, with Q=uu⊤, satisfies the displayed inequality. Expanding u in an orthonormal eigenbasis gives λ1​−u⊤Hu≥γ(1−∣u⊤v∣2), while ∥P−Q∥F2​=2(1−∣u⊤v∣2). The analogous statement for a smallest eigenvalue follows by replacing H by −H.
Rank-one eigenprojector perturbation bound (∥P−P∥F​≤22​∥W∥op​/γ)
Words: 50
Davis-Kahan curvature lemma OurBigBook.com
Let P project onto a leading unit eigenvector of H+W, with H as in the Davis-Kahan curvature lemma. Its maximizing Rayleigh quotient gives tr(H(P−P))≤tr(W(P−P)). Duality of the operator norm and trace norm, together with the rank-two bound ∥P−P∥∗​≤2​∥P−P∥F​, proves the estimate. No gap condition on the perturbed matrix is needed.

A complex matrix is unitary when U†U=UU†=I. Its columns form an orthonormal basis, and it preserves inner products and norms.

Unitary matrix OurBigBook.com
Every unitary matrix has a unique decomposition U=A+iB into Hermitian matrices. The formulas follow by adding and subtracting U and its conjugate transpose. Expanding U†U=UU†=I gives A2+B2+i(AB−BA)=I and A2+B2−i(AB−BA)=I. Therefore the parts commute and A2+B2=I.

The real vector space of traceless skew-Hermitian matrices of size two is the Lie algebra su(2). For the basis M1​=21​diag(i,−i), M2​=21​(0−1​10​), M3​=21​(0i​i0​), cyclic commutators satisfy [M1​,M2​]=M3​. The map a↦∑aj​Mj​ carries the cross product to the commutator. Every target is a single commutator: choose a unit vector perpendicular to its associated vector c and use u×(c×u)=c.

If A is a Hermitian matrix, then (I+iA)−1(I−iA) is unitary. This Cayley transform maps each real eigenvalue λ to the unit-modulus number (1−iλ)/(1+iλ).

Hoffman–Wielandt inequality (minπ​∑i​∣λi​(A)−λπ(i)​(B)∣2≤∥A−B∥F2​)

Words: 82 Articles: 1
Normal matrix OurBigBook.com
For two normal matrices of the same size, a pairing of their eigenvalues has squared Euclidean discrepancy at most the squared Frobenius norm of their difference. For Hermitian matrices, the increasing real eigenvalue order gives such a pairing, because it minimizes squared discrepancy. For real symmetric matrices, the norm square is Tr(A−B)2.

Words: 37
Hoffman–Wielandt inequality OurBigBook.com
For equally sized Hermitian matrices and a real test function with Lipschitz bound one, the difference of its averages under their empirical spectral measures is at most N−1/2 times the Frobenius norm of their difference. Pair the increasing eigenvalues, apply the triangle inequality and Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, then use the Hoffman–Wielandt inequality.

Normal matrix OurBigBook.com
If a normal matrix satisfies Ax=λx, then A†x=λx. Indeed, M=A−λI is normal and ∥Mx∥2=x†M†Mx=x†MM†x=∥M†x∥2. Since Mx=0, also M†x=0. This identity proves orthogonality of distinct eigenspaces and gives spectral restrictions for Hermitian matrices, skew-Hermitian matrices and unitary matrices.

AA†−A†A=(a2−c2ib(a+c)​−ib(a+c)c2−a2​).

Thus the displayed conditions are necessary and sufficient for a normal matrix. In the family a=1, b=c=q, normality requires q=−1, not q=1. Non-normal matrix

Words: 520 Articles: 10
Normal matrix OurBigBook.com
A matrix is non-normal when it does not commute with its adjoint. Its eigenvectors need not be orthogonal, so combinations of individually decaying modes may grow temporarily.

The real matrix BM​=(10​M1​) has both eigenvalues equal to one, whereas xTBM​x/(xTx)=1+M/2 for x=(1,1)T. Hence no universal constant bounds this quotient by the maximum eigenvalue of every real matrix with real eigenvalues.

Transient growth

Words: 464 Articles: 8
Non-normal matrix OurBigBook.com
Transient growth is finite-time amplification in a stable linear system. For a non-normal generator it can occur even when every eigenvalue has negative real part, because nonorthogonal eigenmodes can interfere constructively.

Words: 123 Articles: 1
Transient growth OurBigBook.com
For M=(−1/R1​0−2/R​) with R>0, write s=t/R. Its matrix exponential is B=(aR(a−a2)​0a2​), a=e−s. The maximizing unit initial state is the largest-eigenvalue eigenvector of B∗B. Its component ratio is the displayed expression, with d=(es+1)/(2R)+(R/2)(es−1). This follows by solving the quadratic eigenvector equation for the symmetric two-by-two Gram matrix. The state tends to (1,0)T for t≫R.

Words: 64
Optimal initial state for triangular stable shear OurBigBook.com
In the optimal initial state for triangular stable shear, expansion of et/R gives the displayed leading parameter with relative error O(t/R). Keeping both terms distinguishes a large-R shear regime from the limit t→0 at fixed R. The latter direction is the largest-eigenvalue direction of the Hermitian part of M; the former can instead have large absolute time and substantial shear amplification even though t/R is small.
Instantaneous energy-growth criterion for a linear system
Words: 54
Transient growth OurBigBook.com
For x′=Lx and E=∥x∥22​, the Hermitian matrix H=(L+L∗)/2 gives E˙=2x∗Hx. Thus some initial condition grows immediately iff the largest eigenvalue of H is positive. All trajectories have nonincreasing energy iff H is a negative semidefinite matrix. This differs from requiring negative real parts for the eigenvalues of L: a non-normal matrix can satisfy modal decay while allowing transient growth.

Transient growth OurBigBook.com
For L=(λ1​1​0λ2​​) with distinct real negative eigenvalues, the matrix exponential is A=(ab​0d​), where a=eλ1​t, d=eλ2​t and b=(a−d)/(λ1​−λ2​). The optimal energy amplification of a linear system is

Energy-neutral rotational nonlinearity (xTNx=0,NT=−N)
Words: 56
Two-dimensional triangular model of transient growth OurBigBook.com
A nonlinear term f(∣x∣)Nx with real skew-symmetric matrix N contributes zero to the derivative of the quadratic energy ∣x∣2/2. It changes orientation rather than magnitude directly. If a separate linear generator is a non-normal matrix, that reorientation can still alter later transient growth, so energy cancellation alone does not make the nonlinear evolution equivalent to the linear one.

Rayleigh quotient with one Neumann endpoint (R=k2−[ϕϕ′]z1​z2​​/∫ϕ2dz)

Words: 78
Rayleigh quotient OurBigBook.com
For a nonzero real solution of ϕ′′+(C−k2)ϕ=0 on a finite interval, integration by parts gives R=∫(Cϕ2−ϕ′2)dz/∫ϕ2dz in the displayed form. A Neumann boundary condition only at the lower endpoint does not remove the upper boundary term. Equality with k2 additionally requires ϕ(z2​)ϕ′(z2​)=0. With the lower condition, nonconstant oscillatory solutions satisfy this when their phase advance is an integer multiple of π/2; affine solutions must be constant, while nonzero hyperbolic-cosine solutions fail the condition. Infinite intervals additionally require convergence of both integrals.

Hermitian Rayleigh quotient range ([λmin​,λmax​])

Words: 39
Rayleigh quotient OurBigBook.com
The Rayleigh quotient of a finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix ranges over its smallest-to-largest eigenvalue interval. In an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors it is a weighted average of the eigenvalues, with nonnegative weights summing to one. Combining the extreme eigenvectors with coefficients 1−t​,t​ realizes every value of the interval.

Odd variational trial gives an excited oscillator bound

Words: 35
Rayleigh quotient OurBigBook.com
An odd trial state is orthogonal to the even oscillator ground state. Its Rayleigh quotient therefore bounds the first excited energy from above, unlike an arbitrary trial state. The kinetic quadratic form permits continuous compactly supported trials with derivative jumps.

Generalized Rayleigh quotient (xTBxxTAx​)

Words: 33
Rayleigh quotient OurBigBook.com
For symmetric A and positive-definite B, the generalized Rayleigh quotient is xTAx/(xTBx). Its stationary values are the generalized eigenvalues of Av=λBv, and its maximum is the largest such eigenvalue.

Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle

Words: 203 Articles: 4
Rayleigh quotient OurBigBook.com
The extremal Rayleigh quotients of a self-adjoint operator are the extremal spectral values. In particular, a Hamiltonian with a discrete spectrum satisfies R[ψ]≥E0​, with equality precisely on its ground-state eigenspace. More generally, minimizing over states orthogonal to the first j eigenspaces gives an upper bound on Ej​.

Cyclic vector OurBigBook.com
A cyclic subspace generated by x under a linear operator T is the span of its successive iterates x,Tx,T2x,…. In finite dimension it is already generated by the first n iterates. The endomorphism algebra has dimension d∑a,b​min(a,b)ma​mb​=d∑i​(λi′​)2; its semisimple quotient is ∏j​Mmj​​(Fqd​), and units are precisely lifts of units in that quotient.

Counting matrices with a fixed primary polynomial

Words: 49
Primary matrix centralizer formula OurBigBook.com
Fix an irreducible polynomial f of degree d with nonzero constant term. In GLdm​(q), the number of matrices whose minimal polynomial is a power of f is ∣GLdm​(q)∣qd(m2−m)/∣GLm​(qd)∣. The primary matrix centralizer formula is identical to the unipotent centralizer formula over Fqd​, and summing reciprocal centralizer orders reduces to counting nilpotent matrices by the Fitting decomposition.

For a finite-dimensional vector space regarded as an F[X]-module through a linear operator, the monic invariant factors a1​∣⋯∣ak​ give the decomposition ⨁i​F[X]/(ai​). Their product is the characteristic polynomial and the largest is the minimal polynomial.
